metadata.title: Trigonometry for Shaders
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Turn an angle into a position, and back again
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Trigonometry for Shaders. Learn what sine and cosine really do, then use them to send a moon around a planet and reveal a picture like a clock hand.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most of us met trigonometry as triangles on paper, and forgot it. In a shader it does one job. It turns an angle into a position.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. An angle is an amount of turn. A radian is an angle measured so that a full turn is about six point two eight. The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle. A vec two is a bundle of two numbers. And U V is a pixel's address, zero to one across and down.

'Vec2' lands
'UV' lands

terms.meaning: an amount of turn, in degrees or radians
an angle where a full turn is about 6.28
the longest side of a right triangle
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down

beats.narration_text: A moon circles a planet, and a meteor circles the moon. Nobody animated it by hand. In the shader, an angle goes in, and two numbers come out that say where the moon is. Those numbers come from a triangle.

No code is shown yet.

beats.narration_text: Start with a triangle that has a right angle in one corner. Its longest side is the hypotenuse. Now pick another corner. The side across from it is the opposite side. The side touching it is the adjacent side.

shot.visual_intent: A right triangle in grey outline on the cream stage, right angle at the lower right marked with a small square, the other angles at the lower left (30 degrees, marked by a thick terracotta arc and a small terracotta dot) and the top right. As each word is spoken the matching side thickens to ink and takes a 1 to 3 word serif label placed outside the outline: 'hypotenuse' on the long slanted side, 'opposite' on the right-hand vertical (across from the marked angle), 'adjacent' on the bottom (touching the marked angle). The 50 % frame holds the settled picture with the hypotenuse label and the marked angle.

beats.narration_text: Here is the useful part. Fix the angle, and the ratio of any two sides stays fixed, whatever the size. At thirty degrees, the opposite side is always half the hypotenuse. At fifty, about point seven seven of it.

shot.visual_intent: The same 30-degree triangle anchored at its marked lower-left corner. At the right, a readout in serif: 'opposite ÷ hypotenuse' over a large number. First the triangle scales (about 1.0, then 0.55, then 1.3) while thin grey ghosts of the earlier sizes stay nested at the same corner and the number stays 0.50 the whole time. After a hold (settled still at the 50 % frame: three nested outlines, '30°' and 0.50), the marked angle opens to 50 degrees: the hypotenuse swings up, the triangle reshapes, the angle label reads '50°' and the number settles at 0.77. A terracotta dot rides the top corner.

beats.narration_text: Those ratios have names. Opposite over hypotenuse is the sine. Adjacent over hypotenuse is the cosine. Opposite over adjacent is the tangent. The memory trick is S O H, C A H, T O A.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the 30-degree triangle in grey, smaller. Right: three stacked outlined rows (padding, no fill behind text): 'sine · opposite ÷ hypotenuse', 'cosine · adjacent ÷ hypotenuse', 'tangent · opposite ÷ adjacent'. As each name is spoken its row lands and the two sides it uses thicken to ink on the triangle (sine: opposite and hypotenuse; cosine: adjacent and hypotenuse; tangent: opposite and adjacent) while the others return to grey. At the end 'SOH CAH TOA' sets under the rows with each first letter aligned to its row.

SOH CAH TOA sets under the rows

shot.motion_claim: Two sides of the triangle light up for each ratio as the voice names it.

beats.narration_text: So sine and cosine are lookups. Hand one an angle, and it hands back a ratio. Sine of thirty degrees is one half. Cosine of thirty degrees is about point eight seven. An angle goes in, a number comes out.

shot.visual_intent: Two outlined boxes stacked on the cream stage, labelled 'sine' (upper) and 'cosine' (lower). At the left a small wedge token marked '30°' slides along a short drawn arrow into the sine box; a number token '0.50' slides out at the right. The same 30-degree token then enters the cosine box and '0.87' leaves it. One short line under the boxes: 'angle in, number out'. Arrows are drawn shapes, not glyphs; the 50 % frame holds with the sine result '0.50' settled.

beats.narration_text: Now put that triangle inside a circle. Walk out from the middle at your angle until you reach the circle. The triangle's two short sides say where you stand: so far across, so far up.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Angle In, Position Out' (serif 40) top-left. On paper orientation (y up, a small grey caption 'on paper'): a circle with a faint cross of axes, 'radius 1' on a radius. A radius line sweeps from the right-hand axis up to 30 degrees and a terracotta dot lands on the circle where it ends. Then the triangle from before draws in: a dashed vertical drop from the dot to the horizontal axis and the horizontal leg along the axis. The marked angle is a thick terracotta arc, never a filled wedge.

beats.narration_text: Make the radius one and you have the unit circle. The hypotenuse is one, so dividing by one changes nothing. The opposite side is the sine itself, the adjacent side the cosine itself. The point sits at cosine across, sine up.

shot.visual_intent: The same circle, dot and triangle (paper orientation, y up, as in the previous beat). The tag 'unit circle' lands beside the circle. The horizontal leg takes the label 'cos' and the vertical leg 'sin'; the hypotenuse keeps 'radius 1'. Beside the circle a live readout in serif: 'cos 0.87' over 'sin 0.50'. A faded '÷ 1' on each ratio shrinks away as the voice says dividing by one changes nothing. After a hold (settled at 30 degrees through the midpoint) the angle swings to 60 degrees and back to 30, the legs resizing and both readout numbers following (0.50 and 0.87 at 60 degrees); the point label '(cos, sin)' sits at the dot.

beats.narration_text: Godot's own manual says the same. Vector two has a function, from angle, that builds a point from an angle. The manual calls it equivalent to cosine of the angle, sine of the angle. The engine knows the recipe.

shot.visual_intent: The real Godot 4.7 Vector2 class page scrolled to from_angle(); the camera pushes in on the sentence 'This is equivalent to doing Vector2(cos(angle), sin(angle)) or Vector2.RIGHT.rotated(angle).' and one terracotta ring marks it. The move and ring coordinates are set from the real screenshot at build time.

beats.narration_text: Want a bigger circle? Multiply by the radius. Want it somewhere else? Add the center. So center plus radius times cosine and sine puts a point on a circle of any size, anywhere.

shot.visual_intent: The circle from before (paper orientation, y up) with its terracotta dot at 30 degrees. A formula builds under it, term by term, in the monospace face (32 or larger): 'c + r * vec2(cos(a), sin(a))'. As 'r *' lands the circle grows from radius 1 to 1.8 with the dot riding on it at the same angle; as 'c +' lands the whole circle slides to a new center (a small terracotta cross marks the center and travels with it). The 50 % frame holds the grown and moved circle with the whole formula landed.

beats.narration_text: Try one by hand. Radius point six, angle thirty degrees. The first number is point six times cosine, about point five two. The second is point six times sine, exactly point three. Hold on to those two numbers.

The two results end boxed together as '(0.52, 0.30)' beside the dot with a small grey line 'hold on to these'. Paper orientation (up positive); the dot is not mirrored.

beats.narration_text: One catch. Shaders measure angles in radians, not degrees. Lay one radius along the edge of the circle, and the angle it covers is a radian. A full turn takes a little over six of them: about six point two eight.

shot.visual_intent: A circle (paper orientation, y up) with its radius drawn as a thick ink bar from the middle. The bar copies itself onto the circle's edge as a bent arc of exactly its own length, starting at the right-hand axis; a thick terracotta arc marks the angle it covers, labelled 'radian' (a thick arc, never a filled wedge). Copies lay end to end around the circle while a counter ticks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and a short leftover piece closes the loop; the label ends '6.28 = a full turn'. The 50 % frame holds with about three copies laid and the counter at 3.

beats.narration_text: Godot names the big ones. Pi is half a turn. Tau is a full turn, which is two pi. And the function radians converts degrees, so forty-five degrees comes out as pi over four.

shot.visual_intent: The same circle after the walk (paper orientation: the sweep goes counterclockwise, y up). A radius sweeps once round from the right-hand axis; tick marks land at the quarter points in turn with code-font labels: 'PI / 2' at the top, 'PI' at the left, '3 * PI / 2' at the bottom and 'TAU' back at the start. Then a wedge outline of 45 degrees draws and a line appears beside the circle: 'radians(45.0)' = 'PI / 4.0'. A small grey credit line under it: 'Godot 4.7 docs · Global built-ins'. The 50 % frame holds with the sweep finished and all four labels landed.

beats.narration_text: Skip the conversion and the shader still compiles. That is the trap. Thirty radians is almost five full turns, so sine of thirty comes out near minus one. Convert first, and sine of thirty degrees is one half again.

Right, titled 'sin(radians(30.0))': the dot moves a short way up to a 30-degree mark and its mid-grey bar shows '0.50'. A small grey credit line: 'math values · checked in a Godot 4.7.2 shader'. The 50 % frame holds with the left dot stopped near the bottom and its counter at 4; the left bar settles just after.

beats.narration_text: Why is sine a wave? Plot the point's height against its angle as it goes round. The height climbs to one, falls through zero to minus one, and comes home. That curve is the sine wave.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the circle with its terracotta dot (paper orientation, y up). Right: a plot with the angle along the bottom (faint ticks at pi/2, pi, 3pi/2, tau) and 'height' up the side. As the dot goes once round, a thin dashed line runs from the dot across to the plot and a curve draws behind it: up to 1, back through 0, down to -1, home. The finished curve is labelled 'sine'. The 50 % frame holds with the dot at the left of the circle (half turn) and the curve drawn to pi.

beats.narration_text: Now a shader. It runs once for each pixel, and U V says where that pixel is. Double it and subtract one, and the range becomes minus one to one, with zero, zero in the middle. Call that p.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'An Orbit' (serif 40) top-left. A square drawn the shader way (the second number counts DOWN, small grey 'y' arrow pointing down): corner labels (0, 0) top left and (1, 1) bottom right, a terracotta dot at the middle labelled (0.5, 0.5) and a short tag 'UV'. A small code card lands beside it with 'void fragment() {', the line 'vec2 p = UV * 2.0 - 1.0;' and '}', and a 3-word tag 'once per pixel' on the function line. As the line lands the labels slide to the centered numbers: corners (-1, -1) and (1, 1), middle (0, 0); the dot visits the top-left corner and the middle, showing both numbers. The 50 % frame holds with the line landed and the labels still 0 to 1.

beats.narration_text: On paper, up is positive. On a screen, y counts downward. The formulas stay the same and the picture flips: down is a quarter turn, and a growing angle turns clockwise. Godot's manual agrees.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. An angle fixes the ratios of a right triangle: sine, cosine and tangent. On the unit circle, cosine and sine are the point at an angle: angle in, position out. Shader angles are radians, and a full turn is tau. An orbit is a center, a radius and an angle that grows. A circle's center can itself be on an orbit. Arc tangent runs it backwards: a position gives back its angle.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot canvas item shader for a square Color Rect: a teal planet in the middle and a smaller moon that circles it once every four seconds. Place the moon with cosine and sine of an angle in radians, and point me to the line that sets the speed. Then check two things yourself. Does the moon finish a lap in about four seconds? And does it turn clockwise, so that negating the angle reverses it?
